title: STAR method
examples: How do I use the STAR method for a leadership question?
Can you give me an example of a good 'Result'?
Is the STAR method better than just telling a story?

explain.say: The STAR method helps you answer interview questions well. It gives structure to your experience stories.
First, describe the situation you faced. Set the scene for your story clearly.
Next, explain the specific task you needed to complete. What was the goal you had to achieve?
Then, detail the action you personally took. Focus on what you did, not what the team did.
Finally, state the positive result of your actions. Quantify this result if you can with numbers.

For a real-life example, imagine a time a project was behind schedule. You managed stakeholder expectations by creating a daily progress report, which kept everyone informed and allowed the team to finish two days early.

faq.q: Should I include my whole team's actions in the Action step?
faq.a: No, the Action step must focus on your individual contributions. You need to highlight what you specifically did.
asks: Do I talk about what others did?

faq.q: What if the result wasn't a perfect success?
faq.a: You can still use the method. Focus on what you learned or what you improved for next time. Growth is a good result.

faq.q: How long should my whole answer be using STAR?
faq.a: Aim for a concise answer, usually between one and two minutes. Practice keeping it focused.

faq.q: Does the Situation need to be dramatic or complex?
faq.a: No, it just needs to be a real professional challenge. Keep the situation clear and professional.
asks: Does it have to be a big problem?
Can I use a small example?

faq.q: What if I cannot think of a good example right now?
faq.a: It is okay to pause and say you will think of a strong example later. Preparing several stories helps greatly.

facts: The STAR method structures behavioral interview responses.
Situation sets the background context for the story.
Action must describe your personal contribution, not the group's.
Results should ideally be quantified with data or metrics.

quiz.say: A project deadline was moved up unexpectedly. You organized a shared document system to track all necessary inputs, which helped the team submit the final report two hours early.

options.show: Situation: Project deadline moved up unexpectedly.
options.say: Situation: Project deadline moved up unexpectedly.

options.show: Result: Submitted the final report two hours early.
options.say: Result: Submitted the final report two hours early.

options.show: Task: To complete the project on time.
options.say: Task: To complete the project on time.

quiz.why: The Action step correctly identifies the specific thing you did to solve the problem.

wrong.1: This is the Situation, not the Action. It sets the scene.
wrong.2: This is the Result. It shows the positive outcome.
wrong.3: This is the Task. It states the goal, not what you did.

quiz.say: A client was unhappy with the initial draft. You scheduled a follow-up meeting to gather detailed feedback, which allowed you to revise the proposal and secure the contract.

options.show: Task: To satisfy the unhappy client.
options.say: Task: To satisfy the unhappy client.

options.show: Situation: The client was unhappy with the initial draft.
options.say: Situation: The client was unhappy with the initial draft.

options.show: Action: Scheduled a follow-up meeting to gather feedback.
options.say: Action: Scheduled a follow-up meeting to gather feedback.

quiz.why: The Result step must conclude with the ultimate positive outcome of your efforts.

wrong.0: This is the Task. It defines the immediate goal you needed to achieve.
wrong.2: This is the Situation. It sets up the initial challenge.
wrong.3: This is the Action. It describes the specific step you took.
